places: Hyatt Regency Hotel, Kansas City, Missouri

timeline.event: High unemployment, inflation, and double-digit interest rates put pressure on builders to swiftly complete fast-tracked projects amid nationwide structural failures.
Construction began on the 40-story Hyatt Regency Kansas City.
The Hartford Civic Center roof collapsed.
A 2,700-square-foot section of the Hyatt Regency roof partially collapsed.
The Hyatt Regency hotel officially opened.
The fourth-floor and second-floor walkways collapsed onto partygoers in the hotel lobby during a tea dance.
timeline.place: Hyatt Regency Hotel, Kansas City, Missouri

timeline.event: A laboratory began testing box beams on behalf of the steel fabrication source as an architectural engineer discovered design changes in the walkways.
More than 300 lawsuits seeking a total of $3 billion were filed against parties involved in the hotel's design and operation.
The Hyatt Regency reopened with a redesigned atrium after a committee of engineers and architects concluded there were no other structural safety issues.
The Kansas City Star and the Kansas City Times won a Pulitzer Prize for their 16 months of investigative coverage of the collapse.
Local authorities reported that the $5 million hotel reconstruction made the building possibly the safest in the country.
The disaster was cited in arguments against the Reagan administration's attempt to eliminate an agency of the National Bureau of Standards.
The hotel was renamed the Hyatt Regency Crown Center.

legacy.what: The hotel atrium was redesigned, replacing the second-floor walkway with a column-supported walkway, removing the other walkways permanently, and reinforcing the roof.
The American Society of Civil Engineers adopted a clear policy making structural engineers ultimately responsible for reviewing fabricators' shop drawings.
The Kansas City Codes Administration was turned into its own independent department, doubling its staff and assigning a single engineer to all aspects of each reviewed building.
A $5 million hotel reconstruction was completed, leading local authorities to report the building was possibly the safest in the country.
The disaster was cited in an argument to prevent the Reagan administration from eliminating an agency of the National Bureau of Standards.
The rebuilt hotel was renamed the Hyatt Regency Crown Center.
